articles.title: Bridgend scammer vowed to repay victims but still hasn't a year on
articles.summary: Charlotte Blackwell created a fake wedding to con friends and family to pay off gambling debts.
articles.body:
Victims of a "heartless" fraudster, who faked her own wedding to con relatives and friends out of more than £12,000, are questioning why they have only received a fraction of what she was ordered to pay back.

Charlotte Blackwell, 32, from Bridgend, was handed a suspended prison sentence and ordered to pay £13,750 in compensation to the four victims by a judge in March 2025.

When she realised she would be avoiding jail Blackwell sobbed in relief and agreed to the judge's demand that she pay at a rate of £400 a month.

But her victims say she has only paid a total of £163.

The Ministry of Justice (MOJ) said it could not give specific details on enforcement but added: "These were heartless crimes."

In October 2025, the victims had only received £25.45 each since the order was imposed seven months earlier.

Since that time Blackwell, a mother of two, has paid an additional £15.30 to each of the victims - with no payments made in the last four months.

When the victims asked for updates from the MoJ they said they were told: "It's being dealt with."

"We've sort of given up because there's nowhere for us to turn. It feels like she's being protected rather than the victims."

Blackwell, who was previously spared jail for fraud against a children's cancer charity, made bogus wedding plans in a scheme to pay off her gambling debts.

Between 2022 and 2024 she took £12,682 from members of the supposed wedding party under the pretence it was for a planned ceremony in Turkey.

The four victims were her then-fiancé's mother Paula Thomas, who paid £3,296, and three of Thomas' friends - including Morse, who paid £3,311, Sue Chapman, who paid £3,272, and Tracey Roberts, who paid £2,803.

Blackwell was ordered to pay £3,500 in compensation each to Thomas, Chapman, and Morse, and £3,250 to Roberts to "reflect the additional aggravation and distress" she had caused them.

She was also handed a suspended 12-month jail term, 120 hours of unpaid work and five days of rehabilitation activity.

Her barrister Alice Sykes said her client would be able to pay the compensation, as she was working full-time as an estate agent on £1,700 a month, as well as receiving universal credit.

Blackwell was back in court in October 2025 after being fined for breaching her community service order .

Morse, an admin worker at a GP surgery, previously said: "When Charlotte got engaged to Paula's son Daniel we all welcomed her, we went out with her a few times, and it turned out she was taking money from us for a wedding that didn't exist.

"At one point we wondered why she hadn't bought her wedding dress because it wasn't long before the wedding date and we were saying: 'You need to get a move on.'

"She then cancelled the wedding saying she was ill. But I was 50 that year so my partner and I still wanted to go to Turkey."

Morse went into the travel agency Blackwell had supposedly used, Tui, and asked staff for the details of the holiday.

She said the staff were trying to "ring a wedding coordinator who didn't exist" and spent an hour trying to help her, but came back to tell her nothing had been booked.

"You trust people don't you? This has made us really cautious now in everything we do. It's sad but we feel like we wouldn't trust anybody again."

Morse, who had taken a second job as a cleaner to help pay for the bogus holiday, said: "It's very frustrating because, as victims, we should surely be informed of what's going on but we get the same non-answer every time we chase the Ministry of Justice."

The fraud included fake flight confirmations, fake emails from travel agents and fake bank transactions.

Blackwell even created fake email accounts to make it seem like she had been communicating with agents.

Sykes said: "She was going through a difficult time after her daughter had been diagnosed with brain cancer.

"She gave up work to deal with the money issues that came with that and gambled to try to get money back. She then placed blocks on websites to prevent gambling and has taken steps to prevent that happening again."

Blackwell avoided jail in August 2024, and was instead handed a suspended 10-month prison sentence, 180 hours of unpaid work, 10 days of rehabilitation activity, and a four-month curfew preventing her from leaving home at night after defrauding children's charity, Morgan's Army of £4,000.

Morgan's Army was set up by the parents of Morgan Ridler, who died of cancer aged three. It supports south Wales families affected by childhood cancer.

Months after Morgan's death in June 2023, Blackwell lied to the charity saying her daughter needed costly treatment in Germany, when in reality she was in remission from cancer.

After the deception was discovered the money was frozen and recovered.

The MoJ said it could not give specific details on enforcement due to data protection laws but said: "These were heartless crimes. We take the recovery and enforcement of financial penalties very seriously as we know how important it is that victims get what they are owed.

"We can take money directly from an offender's benefits or salaries or issue a warrant to seize offender's possessions if needed."

articles.title: Dolly Parton prayed in backyard church before recording comeback album, Ricky Skaggs says
articles.summary: Ricky Skaggs reveals how he and Dolly Parton prayed at a tiny rebuilt church in her backyard before recording their hit album "White Limozeen."
articles.body: Ricky Skaggs is recalling how he and Dolly Parton prayed at the altar of a tiny church rebuilt in her backyard before recording the country comeback album that would help return her to the top of the charts. During an interview with Fox News Digital, the 72-year-old bluegrass and country star remembered working on 1989's "White Limozeen" with the late music icon, who died on Aug. 25 at the age of 80. Prior to making "White Limozeen," Skaggs told Fox News Digital that he visited Parton at her home in Nashville, where the two shared a private, faith-filled moment. DOLLY PARTON'S LIFE IN HER OWN WORDS: FROM SMOKY MOUNTAINS POVERTY TO COUNTRY MUSIC IMMORTALITY "She took me out in the backyard and showed me this little church that she used to go to when she was a kid up in East Tennessee. They had torn it down and they numbered all the slats and all the flooring and everything like that. They brought it down to her backyard and rebuilt it into a beautiful little church," Skaggs recalled. "She wanted me to go in," he continued. "We went in there and they had a little piano in there and a little altar, just like the old Baptist churches in the mountains. So we got up by the altar and just started praying after talking in there for a while about our faith. And we asked God’s hand to be on this record, that he would bless it, bless the musicians, bless all the singers." CARRIE UNDERWOOD HONORS DOLLY PARTON'S FAITH AND LEGACY DURING EMOTIONAL CONCERT TRIBUTE "I just never have forgotten just the power of that day," Skaggs added. "That whole day was just wonderful. It showed me the kind of woman she was." Skaggs recalled how he teamed up with Parton on "White Limozeen" after she invited him to produce the album following an appearance by the singer and his country band on her Los Angeles-based television show "Dolly." WATCH: DOLLY PARTON PRAYED AT BACKYARD ALTAR BEFORE COMEBACK ALBUM, RICKY SKAGGS SAYS DOLLY PARTON DEFIED COUNTRY MUSIC'S EXPECTATIONS FOR WOMEN AND BUILT A CAREER ON HER OWN TERMS: EXPERTS "I came up and hugged her 'bye' and told her I really appreciate her having us on the show. And I said, ‘By the way, when are you going to do a real country album again?’" he remembered. Skaggs continued, "She said, ‘Well, I’ve been thinking a lot about that. And I think I really want to do a country record. But I want you to produce it.’ I said, ‘What?'" STEVE DOOCY: THE DOLLY PARTON I SAW WHEN THE CAMERAS STOPPED ROLLING "I was shocked to the bone," he admitted. "That was one of the most mind-blowing, waking up smelling the roses kind of thing that I'd ever had happen at that time, musically for sure. But that was just being the right person in the right place at the right time around the right person." "Only God could make those things happen." DOLLY PARTON'S MOST ICONIC 'DOLLY-ISMS' ON BEAUTY, WIGS, BOTOX AND LIVING LIFE ON HER OWN TERMS After rising to global fame as a country singer, Parton spent much of the late 1970s and 1980s broadening into pop-influenced material. Prior to "White Limozeen," she released her 1987 solo album "Rainbow," which was a critical and commercial disappointment. "Rainbow," which marked her most overtly pop-leaning solo album, struggled to find an audience, peaking at No. 18 on Billboard’s Top Country Albums and failing to produce a Top 40 country single. With "White Limozeen," Skaggs brought Parton back to a more traditional country sound. The album became a hit, reaching No. 3 on Billboard’s Top Country Albums chart, yielding two No. 1 country hits, "Why’d You Come in Here Lookin’ Like That" and "Yellow Roses," and earning a Gold certification from the RIAA. DOLLY PARTON'S BELOVED LITERACY MISSION SEES SURGE OF SUPPORT AFTER COUNTRY ICON'S DEATH Although "White Limozeen" remained their only major recording collaboration, Skaggs said he and Parton shared a lasting bond rooted in their Appalachian backgrounds and Christian faith. The Kentucky native said Parton lived out her beliefs through compassion and generosity, even though some were critical of her glamorous image. BROADCAST BIAS: DOLLY PARTON TAUGHT THE WORLD THE WAY TO BE UNIVERSALLY BELOVED "Some religious people would have really, and probably did, judge her for the way she wore her clothes, or the way that she did this and that and the other, but man, she reflected the love of Jesus everywhere she was," he said. "She did so much for the homeless, for the poor, for hurting people." "She used what God had given her with her talent and her gifts, but she used that for His advantage, I mean, to show God's love to people that didn't feel loved by the world or by others, even other Christians," Skaggs continued. "And I just, I loved her for that. And I've really thought a lot about that since her passing." BIG & RICH SAY DOLLY PARTON PUT FAME ASIDE TO HELP NEIGHBORS AFTER 2016 TENNESSEE WILDFIRES Throughout her life, Parton was known for her philanthropy, which spanned literacy, disaster relief and medical research. In 1995, she launched the Imagination Library, a program that gifted hundreds of millions of free, age-appropriate books to children from birth to age 5 worldwide. The 11-time Grammy Award winner also established the My People Fund after the 2016 Great Smoky Mountains wildfires, providing eligible Sevier County families whose homes were destroyed with $1,000 a month for up to six months. In 2020, Parton donated $1 million to Vanderbilt University Medical Center for COVID-19 research. While speaking with Fox News Digital, Skaggs reflected on how the moment he shared with Parton in her backyard church had stayed with him and influenced his own band's pre-show ritual. articles.title: Woman died of heatstroke climbing Yr Wyddfa, inquest hears
articles.summary: Sophie Goodyer-Bird, 35, died while climbing Yr Wyddfa in July, an inquest opening hears.
articles.body:
A 35-year-old woman died of heatstroke on Wales' highest mountain, an inquest has heard.

Sophie Goodyer-Bird, from Birmingham, was climbing Yr Wyddfa - also known as Snowdon - on 10 July, a few days after her birthday.

On Wednesday, an inquest opening at Caernarfon Coroners' Court heard Goodyer-Bird became increasingly tired while coming down the mountain.

Near the end of the walk, she became unresponsive, and was confirmed to have died shortly afterwards.

Coroner Kate Robertson said emergency services were called and attempted CPR, but were unable to revive her.

A provisional cause of death was given as exertional heat stroke.

The inquest was adjourned to a full hearing, which will take place at a later date.

Following her death, an online fundraiser was set up to raise money for her 12-year-old son.

articles.title: Dale 'Grey Beard' Sanders reclaims title as oldest person to thru-hike the Appalachian Trail at 91
articles.summary: Dale "Grey Beard" Sanders reclaimed his own Appalachian Trail age record at 91, surviving 71 falls across 2,200 miles to summit Mount Katahdin.
articles.body: In case you were feeling particularly productive and accomplished today, a man named Dale "Grey Beard" Sanders is about to humble you. At 91-years-old, Sanders officially reclaimed his title Monday as the oldest person ever to complete a thru-hike of the Appalachian Trail, finishing his journey atop Mount Katahdin in Maine. And before we go any further, understand that hiking the Appalachian Trail is an extraordinary feat for any hiker — let alone someone with nine decades under his belt. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS The AT stretches roughly 2,200 miles from Springer Mountain in Georgia to Katahdin in Maine, crossing 14 states along the way. According to the Appalachian Trail Conservancy, hikers who complete the whole thing experience about 464,500 feet of elevation gain— and an equal amount of loss. That combined 929,000 feet of elevation change is equal to going from sea level to the top of Mount Everest and back roughly 16 times. And here I was proud of myself for taking the stairs at the airport. The Appalachian Trail is absolutely brutal The distance alone is obviously absurd, but mileage is only part of what makes the AT such a beast. Unlike some long-distance trails that offer extended stretches of relatively forgiving terrain, the AT spends much of its length going relentlessly up and down the Appalachian Mountains. Hikers contend with steep climbs, boulder fields, exposed roots, mud, stream crossings and rocks upon rocks upon rocks. CLIMBING EL CAPITAN WHILE NEARLY BLIND: WHY EITAN ARMON REFUSED TO SIT AROUND WAITING FOR A CURE Then you reach New Hampshire's White Mountains and Maine, where the trail gets particularly rude. Southern Maine and the Whites are considered among the most difficult portions of the AT, with steep ascents and descents and rugged terrain. And before hikers can officially call themselves finishers on a northbound journey, they still have to deal with Katahdin — a mountain that requires more than 4,000 feet of climbing and stretches of scrambling over boulders and ledges. Consider that the grand finale. And Sanders did it at 91 years old. According to the Associated Press, he fell just 200 yards from the finish. It was his 71st fall of the journey. Six of those were what Sanders considered "hard falls," including one that eventually resulted in a brief hospitalization. Here’s where the story gets crazier. Dale Sanders has broken this record twice. Sanders didn't just break the Appalachian Trail age record. He reclaimed his own record. Back in 2017, Grey Beard completed the trail at age 82, becoming the oldest person to do it at the time. His record stood until 2021, when his friend M.J. "Nimblewill Nomad" Eberhart finished at 83. 14 TAILGATING ESSENTIALS FOR GRILLING, WATCHING THE GAME AND STAYING WARM Sanders actually helped Eberhart during that record-setting hike, joining his friend for some difficult stretches when Eberhart was considering quitting. But then, Sanders decided he wanted his title back. He started this latest attempt from Harpers Ferry, West Virginia, on Sept. 6, 2025, hiking south toward Georgia before taking the winter off. He returned in the spring and headed north from Harpers Ferry toward Maine, targeting about 12 miles per day with one rest day each week. The Appalachian Trail Conservancy allows thru-hikers to complete sections in different orders and take breaks, provided the entire trail is completed within a year. Sanders finished in 359 days. Fun fact: Sanders was born in 1935. The Appalachian Trail wasn't completed until 1937. The man is literally older than the trail he just hiked. Grey Beard has no interest in acting his age Sanders has spent his later years collecting endurance accomplishments that would exhaust most people half his age. He has paddled the entire Mississippi River — more than once — and became the oldest person to complete the trip when he did it at 87. He's also set an age record on the Grand Canyon's grueling rim-to-rim-to-rim route. Still, this Appalachian Trail attempt wasn't easy even by Grey Beard standards. During a June descent of Vermont's Killington Mountain, Sanders went down in a boulder field hard enough to bloody his arms and legs. Weeks later, numbness in his left arm sent him to a hospital, where what was initially feared to be a stroke turned out to be a pinched nerve. He briefly considered abandoning the attempt before eventually returning to finish the job. So, fellow adventurers, the next time you're 20 minutes into a hike, staring at a switchback and wondering whether you really need to see what's at the top, just remember Grey Beard. articles.title: El 'simpa' de 7.000 euros en un restaurante de Galicia reabre un debate: el camarero responsable de la mesa no está legalmente obligado a pagarlo de su bolsillo
articles.standfirst: Un grupo celebra un cumpleaños y se va sin abonar la cuenta
articles.summary: Un grupo celebra un cumpleaños y se va sin abonar la cuenta
articles.body: La hostelería es el sector por excelencia donde, más allá de los enfrentamientos entre clientes y trabajadores, se producen más situaciones complejas a la hora de abonar la cuenta. La práctica conocida popularmente como ‘simpa’, que consiste básicamente en marcharse del local sin pagar, ha ido más allá en Galicia, ya que dejaron a deber nada menos que 7.000 euros. La propiedad del restaurante Tropicaña, en Orro (Culleredo), confió en la palabra de una madre que, tras contar que había atravesado una mala racha, aseguró que abonaría la cuenta de madrugada, pero nunca lo hizo y dejó al local con un severo problema que acabó con una denuncia. Carol Sao Luis, dueña del restaurante, cuenta a La Voz de Galicia que la mujer pagó los 500 euros de fianza tras haber contratado todos los servicios extra. Más de 80 personas acudieron al evento, que contaba incluso con hinchables para los pequeños. A la hora de pagar, explicó la madre que había discutido con su pareja, que era quien tenía el dinero, y que de madrugada pagaría. Como previsión, hizo una foto de la matrícula del coche. “Los ‘simpas’ son demasiado habituales”, sostiene. Este caso ha provocado que se reabra un eterno debate acerca de si un camarero, responsable de una mesa, debe ser responsable del impago de una cuenta. Lo cierto es que es completamente ilegal que la propiedad obligue a pagar de su bolsillo, o de sus propinas, ya que es el empresario quien asume el riesgo y las posibles pérdidas. El propio Estatuto de los Trabajadores, en su artículo 58.3, sostiene que queda prohibido descontar dinero del salario a un trabajador como sanción o castigo. Si un cliente estafa a un local, es la empresa quien asume el rol de víctima y no el camarero, que no es en ningún caso responsable.

articles.body: El divorico musical del emblemático dúo musical Andy y Lucas no se alcanzó de forma amigable, lo que hacía prever diversos enfrentamientos entre ellos. Y así ha sido. El nuevo capítulo de distanciamiento se ha producido a través de Lucas González, quien ha expresado públicamente su malestar con su compañero, admitiendo que le dolió descubrir que este preparaba un proyecto musical en solitario a sus espaldas. A través de mensajes enviados a Alexia Rivas, colaboradora del programa de televisión ‘El verano se mueve’, el cantante gaditano ha manifestado su decepción con la falta de transparencia de Andrés Morales (Andy) en la gestión de su nueva andadura musical. "A ver si saca su disco de una vez y me deja tranquilo", ha escrito el artista según la tertuliana del formato. “Quien ha acudido a numerosos programas de televisión ha sido él, haciendo afirmaciones que considero que han afectado profundamente a mi honor y mi dignidad”, ha expresado Lucas. Sin embargo, lo que más tristeza le ha producido es enterarse por sí mismo de los planes musicales de su compañero con la confianza que tenían. "Lo que sí me dolió especialmente fue descubrir que después de haber acordado hacer un parón para que yo pudiera operarme de mi primera operación de nariz se estuviera preparando un proyecto a mis espaldas. Creo que después de tantos años compartidos merecía al menos sinceridad y lealtad", ha señalado. Finalmente, el cantante ha lanzado un mensaje contundente: "Quiero dejar algo muy claro: yo no he iniciado esta exposición pública ni he construido ningún discurso contra nadie. Si ahora respondo a determinadas afirmaciones, lo hago exclusivamente para defenderme, proteger mi nombre y contar mi parte cuando considero que se está cuestionando mi honor o mi dignidad. Yo tengo la conciencia tranquila y seguiré mi camino sin necesidad de destruir la imagen de nadie para construir la mía".
